story: James Parkinson called it the shaking palsy in 1817 and noted he had studied some of his cases only by watching them in the street. His name was attached decades later by a French neurologist who thought he deserved it.

Alois Alzheimer's first case was a woman named Auguste Deter, who told him: I have lost myself. He kept her file, and when he examined her brain after death he found the plaques and tangles that still define the disease.

Thomas Hodgkin described seven cases in 1832 and nobody noticed for thirty years. Another doctor read the paper later, confirmed it, and insisted the disease carry Hodgkin's name — a rare act of credit in medical history.

An entire family of cancers defined by what they are not. Once Hodgkin's type could be identified under a microscope, every other lymphoma had to be grouped somewhere — and got a name built out of a negative.

Burrill Crohn published with two colleagues in 1932, and the paper listed authors alphabetically. Crohn came first. His two co-authors, Ginzburg and Oppenheimer, did the same work and are remembered by almost nobody.

Harvey Cushing essentially invented brain surgery as a survivable procedure, cutting mortality from around 90 per cent to under 10. The hormone disorder named after him is a footnote in a career mostly spent elsewhere.

John Langdon Down wrote the first careful clinical description in 1866. His original name for it was withdrawn in the 1960s as both inaccurate and offensive, and the condition was renamed for the doctor instead.

George Huntington described the disease at twenty-two, in the only medical paper he ever published. He had seen it in families on Long Island, where his father and grandfather had also practised — three generations of doctors watching the same households.

Robert Graves was an Irish physician who also introduced the radical idea that feverish patients should be given food and water rather than starved. He suggested his epitaph should read: he fed fevers.

Hakaru Hashimoto published his findings in German in 1912, as a young doctor, and then returned to rural Japan to run a country practice. His work was overlooked for twenty years before anyone realised what he had found.

Thomas Addison worked out that the small glands sitting on top of the kidneys were essential to life — before anyone knew what hormones were. Colleagues found him difficult; patients found him extraordinary.
Richard Bright discovered he could detect kidney disease by heating a patient's urine over a candle and watching for a cloud of albumin. It was one of the first bedside chemical tests in medicine.

James Paget has two different diseases named after him, plus a professorship and a hospital ward. He also worked out, as a student, that the tiny specks in bad pork were a parasite — a finding his professors ignored.

Prosper Meniere showed that vertigo could come from the inner ear rather than the brain, which overturned the standard view. He published it in 1861 and died the following year, before the profession accepted it.

Kinnier Wilson described a disease in which copper builds up in the body until it damages the liver and brain. It is one of the few inherited neurological disorders that can be treated — if it is caught in time.

Charles Bell mapped which nerves carry movement and which carry sensation, work so foundational that a whole law of neurology carries his name too. The sudden facial paralysis is what most people know him for.

Thomas Hodgkin's name attaches to a lymphoma, a clinical sign, and a form of anaemia. He was also a Quaker campaigner who lost a hospital post partly for his outspoken views on the treatment of indigenous peoples.
Stroke the sole of an adult's foot and the toes curl down. If they fan upward instead, something is wrong with the pathway from the brain. Babinski found a whole diagnosis hiding in one reflex.
Stand with your feet together and close your eyes. If you sway, you were relying on sight to stay upright rather than on your body's own position sense. Romberg turned that into a test in the 1840s.

Jozef Brudzinski found that lifting the head of a patient with meningitis makes the knees pull up involuntarily — the body protecting inflamed membranes. He described several such signs; this is the one that kept his name.

Vladimir Kernig noticed that patients with meningitis could not have their leg straightened once the hip was bent. Paired with Brudzinski's sign, it gave doctors a bedside test decades before spinal taps were routine.

Press under the ribs on the right and ask the patient to breathe in. If they stop short from the pain, the gallbladder is inflamed. John Murphy was a Chicago surgeon known for tests that needed no equipment at all.

Charles McBurney worked out that appendicitis pain settles at one specific spot, about two-thirds of the way from the navel to the hip bone. Surgeons still press exactly there, and still call it McBurney's point.
Virginia Apgar sketched five checks on a scrap of paper in a hospital cafeteria after a student asked how to judge a newborn quickly. It is now done on virtually every baby born in a hospital.

Henry Heimlich published the technique in 1974 and it was saving lives within weeks. He was ninety-six when he reportedly used it in a real emergency for the first time, on a fellow resident of his retirement home.
Frederic Foley's design added a small balloon that inflates once the catheter is in place, so it stays put without strapping. He lost the patent fight to a rival, but kept the name.

George Papanicolaou spent twenty years being ignored. His test could catch cervical cancer before symptoms appeared, and the profession did not want it. Once adopted, deaths from the disease fell by around seventy per cent.

Robert Koch set out four conditions that must all hold before you can blame a specific microbe for a specific disease. It is a rule for not fooling yourself, and it ended centuries of guesswork about contagion.

Hans Christian Gram published his staining method in 1884 and wrote that it was imperfect and would surely be improved by others. It has not been. Bacteria are still sorted into Gram-positive and Gram-negative today.

Tuberculosis bacteria have a waxy coat that shrugs off ordinary dyes. Ziehl and Neelsen worked out how to force the stain in with heat and acid, making the bacteria visible as bright red rods under the microscope.
Gustav Giemsa refined a dye mixture that colours the nucleus and cytoplasm of blood cells differently. It is still the standard way of finding malaria parasites in a drop of blood.

Engvall and Perlmann built a test that uses an enzyme to make an invisible immune reaction visible as a colour change. It underpins pregnancy tests, HIV screening, and most rapid tests you have ever used.

Stephen Boyden put a porous membrane between two fluid compartments so he could watch cells crawl through it toward a chemical signal. It is a simple piece of equipment that turned cell migration into something measurable.

Before Petri, cultures were grown under bell jars that had to be lifted, letting in whatever was floating past. His two-part dish with an overlapping lid solved contamination with no moving parts at all.
Emil Erlenmeyer gave the flask sloping sides and a narrow neck, so it can be swirled hard without spilling and stoppered easily. It is the shape everyone draws when asked to draw a chemistry flask.
Ernst Buchner's funnel has a flat perforated plate instead of a cone, so suction can pull liquid through a filter fast. It is the difference between filtering in minutes and filtering overnight.
James Dewar built a double-walled vessel with a vacuum between the layers to hold liquid gases. He never patented it. A German glassware firm did, sold it as the Thermos, and made the fortune.

A glass tube drawn to a fine point, plugged with cotton, sterilised by flame — Pasteur's answer to moving liquid without carrying microbes along with it. The plastic version in every lab still carries his name.

Geiger's early detectors had to be watched, hour after hour, counting faint flashes on a screen in a darkened room. He built the clicking tube partly so physicists could stop staring and start listening.

Christian Doppler predicted the effect in 1842 using starlight. Three years later a Dutch scientist tested it by hiring a train, filling an open carriage with trumpeters, and having musicians on the platform write down what they heard.

Edwin Hall found that a magnetic field pushes a current sideways inside a conductor, producing a small voltage across it. He was a graduate student at the time, testing something Maxwell had said was impossible.

On a spinning planet, anything moving in a straight line appears to curve. It steers hurricanes and long-range artillery. It does not steer water down a plughole — that scale is far too small, whatever you have been told.

A spinning ball drags air around with it, and the uneven airflow pushes it sideways. Heinrich Magnus was investigating why cannonballs curved off target; footballers have been exploiting the same physics ever since.

Daniel Bernoulli found that fast-moving fluid exerts less pressure than slow-moving fluid. He came from a family of mathematicians so competitive that his own father, jealous of a prize, threw him out of the house.
Bounce a radio wave off something moving and it comes back at a shifted frequency — so you can measure speed, not just position. It is why forecasters can see a storm rotating before a tornado forms.

William Thomson worked out there is a coldest possible temperature, where molecular motion stops, and built a scale starting there. He was made Lord Kelvin after the river running past his Glasgow laboratory.

Anders Celsius put 0 at boiling and 100 at freezing — the exact reverse of today's scale. It was flipped after his death, and the version everyone now uses is upside down from the one he actually proposed.

Fahrenheit set his zero at the coldest temperature he could reliably reproduce: a mixture of ice, water and salt. That is why the scale's landmarks look so arbitrary — they were pinned to what he could make in a bucket.
Beaufort's scale needs no instruments — each step is defined by what the sea and the sails are doing. Force 12 was originally described as that which no canvas could withstand.

Halley noticed that comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 followed the same path, decided they were one object, and predicted its return in 1758. He died in 1742. It arrived on Christmas night, sixteen years after his death.

Hubble measured how fast galaxies are moving away and found the farther ones move faster — which means the universe is expanding. Astronomers still cannot agree on the exact number, and the disagreement has a name: the Hubble tension.

Launched in 1990 with a mirror ground to the wrong shape by an amount thinner than a human hair. Astronauts flew up in 1993 and fitted it with corrective optics — effectively giving a telescope a pair of spectacles.

Kepler spent years trying to fit Mars's orbit to a circle and failing by an eight-minute discrepancy he refused to ignore. Those eight minutes broke two thousand years of circular astronomy and gave him the ellipse.

Copernicus reportedly received the first printed copy of his book on the day he died. Moving the Sun to the centre was not just astronomy — it was the moment humanity stopped being the centre of anything.
Giovanni Cassini spotted a dark gap in Saturn's rings in 1675 — the first hint that the rings were not one solid sheet. The spacecraft sent to Saturn three centuries later was named after him.
Jan Oort proposed an enormous shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system, a thousand times farther out than Pluto, purely from the way long-period comets arrive. Nobody has ever seen it.

A ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, and the reason Pluto was reclassified — once astronomers found Pluto had thousands of neighbours out there, it looked less like a planet and more like the largest of a crowd.

Two astronomers independently plotted stars by brightness against temperature and found they do not scatter randomly — they fall into a narrow band. That band is the life story of a star, drawn on one chart.

Chandrasekhar calculated the limit at nineteen, on the boat to England. Eddington, the most famous astronomer alive, publicly ridiculed it. He was right and Eddington was wrong, and he received the Nobel Prize fifty-three years later.

Hubble sorted galaxies by shape into a diagram shaped like a tuning fork — ellipticals on the handle, spirals branching into two prongs. He thought it showed how galaxies evolve. It does not, but the classification stuck.

Charles Messier was hunting comets and kept being fooled by fuzzy things that turned out not to be comets. He catalogued them as a list of objects to ignore — and that list of annoyances is now the most-used catalogue in amateur astronomy.

Patrick Moore noticed Messier's catalogue missed many fine objects, so he made a companion list. He could not use M for Moore, since Messier had it — so he used the other half of his surname, Caldwell.

Get close enough to a planet and its gravity pulls harder on your near side than your far side, until the difference tears you apart. Saturn's rings sit inside Saturn's Roche limit, which is very likely how they formed.
Around each star in a close pair is a teardrop-shaped region where its gravity still wins. Fill that region and matter spills across to the companion — which is how some stars slowly eat each other.

A numerical pattern that seemed to predict planetary distances, and even pointed to a gap where the asteroid belt was later found. Then Neptune was discovered in the wrong place and the whole thing collapsed. It was never a law.

Walter Hohmann worked out the cheapest route between two orbits in 1925 — two engine burns and a long coast. Every mission to Mars still uses it, which is why launch windows come round only every twenty-six months.

Five spots where the pull of two large bodies balances so a small object can sit still relative to both. The James Webb telescope parks at one of them, a million miles out, permanently shaded from the Sun.

Daniel Kirkwood noticed empty lanes in the asteroid belt and worked out why: any asteroid orbiting in a simple ratio with Jupiter gets a repeated nudge at the same point until it is flung out. Resonance clears the road.
A gas cloud is a contest between gravity pulling in and pressure pushing out. James Jeans worked out the mass at which gravity wins — and that threshold is where every star in the universe begins.

A star can only be so bright before its own light blows its outer layers off. Eddington calculated the ceiling — the same Eddington who told the young Chandrasekhar his white-dwarf limit was nonsense.
